caption:
What caused the Tunguska explosion of 1908? The largest explosion in recorded history flattened 2,150 km² of Siberian forest — and never left an impact crater.

On 30 June 1908, something burst in the sky above the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia. It knocked down an estimated 80 million trees, splayed outward from a single point like spokes on a wheel.

The region was so remote that no scientist reached it for 19 years. When Leonid Kulik finally arrived in 1927, he was looking for a crater. He never found one.

The reason: it never hit the ground. The object broke apart roughly 8 km up and dumped its energy into the air as a shockwave. At the very centre, trees were left standing — stripped of branches, but upright — because the blast came straight down on top of them.

What is still open: nobody has ever recovered a fragment. Rock or ice, we don't know.

Photographs: Kulik expedition, May 1929; Sibirskaya Zhizn, July 1908; survey map and terrain photographs, 1930–31. All public domain, colour graded.
